sentence: A reliever inhaler eases symptoms when they happen; a preventer is used daily to calm airway inflammation. They do different jobs.
note: Reliever relieves symptoms when they occur; preventer used daily to reduce airway inflammation (as body[0]).

sentence: The NHS describes a reliever (such as blue salbutamol) as relieving symptoms when they occur and a preventer (a steroid such as beclometasone) as used every day to reduce airway inflammation.
note: As body[0], body[1].

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says asthma guidelines do not recommend a blue reliever on its own, and suggests asking about a preventer or an AIR inhaler.
note: As body[2].

sentence: The NHS says to rinse the mouth or brush the teeth after a steroid inhaler to help prevent infections and a sore mouth; a spacer can help too.
note: As body[3] and body[4].

sentence: Needing a reliever more often than usual can be a sign that asthma is not well controlled, according to the NHS and Asthma + Lung UK, and a GP or asthma nurse can review treatment.
note: As body[5].

sentence: In an asthma attack the NHS and Asthma + Lung UK say to call 999 if the reliever is not helping; NHS 111 and the GP cover non-urgent questions.
note: As body[6].

sentence: The NHS says the main treatment for asthma is medicine breathed in through an inhaler, and that for most people these medicines work well to reduce or prevent symptoms.
note: Search result for NHS asthma pages: main treatment is inhaled medicines that work well for most people to reduce or prevent symptoms.

sentence: A reliever inhaler is used when symptoms appear, and it quickly relaxes the airways so breathing becomes easier.
note: Reliever used when symptoms appear; quickly relaxes the airways (NHS asthma treatment; Asthma + Lung UK reliever page).

sentence: A preventer inhaler is used every day, even when a person feels well, to help stop symptoms starting by reducing swelling and inflammation in the airways.
note: Preventer used every day even when well, reduces inflammation to stop symptoms starting. The wording 'every day, even when well' came partly from an A&E leaflet and the NHS beclometasone page; blended summary.

sentence: The two do different jobs, and the NHS says a reliever is not meant to be given on its own when a preventer has also been prescribed.
note: Summary of NHS asthma treatment said a blue reliever should not be given on its own when a preventer is also prescribed; blended summary, page not named exactly.

sentence: A reliever opens the airways but does not treat the swelling underneath, because relievers contain no steroid.
note: Search summary: relievers contain no steroid so cannot treat airway inflammation; daily steroid preventer helps prevent inflammation.

sentence: Salbutamol, the usual blue reliever, is a bronchodilator, meaning a medicine that widens the airways.
note: NHS salbutamol and bronchodilator pages returned; NHS describes bronchodilators as loosening the muscles lining the airways. Blue colour from Asthma + Lung UK reliever page.

sentence: A preventer such as beclometasone is an inhaled steroid, and the NHS says it needs to be used every day for it to work, even when there are no symptoms.
note: Search summary of NHS beclometasone pages: medicine must be used every day for it to work, even with no symptoms.

sentence: Because a preventer works by calming inflammation, it does not help during an attack.
note: Inferred from preventer reducing inflammation and reliever being the symptom treatment; flagged by author as close to textbook.

sentence: In COPD, the NHS says short-acting bronchodilator inhalers are usually the first treatment, and a steroid inhaler may be added later for people who stay breathless or have frequent flare-ups.
note: Search summary of NHS COPD treatment: short-acting bronchodilators first; steroid inhaler may be suggested if still breathless on long-acting inhaler or frequent flare-ups, normally in a combination inhaler.

sentence: A reliever is used when symptoms occur, while a preventer is part of a daily routine.
note: Reliever as needed; preventer daily.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says current asthma guidelines do not recommend giving anyone with asthma only a blue reliever, and it suggests people ask a GP or asthma nurse about a preventer or an anti-inflammatory reliever, known as AIR.
note: Search summary: Asthma + Lung UK says latest guidelines do not recommend prescribing only a blue reliever; suggests asking GP about preventer or switching to AIR inhaler combining steroid with formoterol.

sentence: The exact medicine, device and plan are set by the prescriber, and the NHS says a person with asthma should have a written asthma action plan.
note: Search summary stated a written asthma action plan from the doctor; prescriber individualises details.

sentence: Stopping or changing a preventer without advice is not recommended, so questions about this go to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.
note: Search summary: guidance says not to stop or change preventer without medical advice; Easyhaler leaflet said patients should not stop treatment unless told to. Route to GP/pharmacist is the author's signposting.

sentence: A spacer is a plastic chamber or tube that fits onto a pressurised metered-dose inhaler, the kind that sprays out a puff of medicine.
note: NHS asthma search summary: spacer is a plastic tube attached to a metered-dose inhaler. Asthma + Lung UK spacers page covers spacers.

sentence: The NHS says a spacer helps more of the medicine reach the lungs and makes the inhaler easier to use.
note: Search summary of NHS asthma page: spacer helps more medicine reach the lungs and makes the inhaler easier to use.

sentence: Dry powder inhalers do not need one.
note: Search summary: dry powder inhalers do not need a spacer.

sentence: The NHS says children and young people should always use their inhaler with a spacer.
note: Search summary: children and young people should always use their inhaler with a spacer.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says a GP, nurse or pharmacist should show a person how to use their inhaler and spacer, and technique can also be checked at the annual asthma review.
note: Spacers page: GP, nurse or pharmacist should show how to use inhaler and spacer; technique can be checked at annual asthma review.

sentence: It also says a whistling sound from the spacer means the person is breathing in too fast.
note: Search summary of spacer videos: a whistling sound means breathing in too fast.

sentence: Yes, the NHS says to rinse the mouth or brush the teeth after using a steroid inhaler, to help prevent mouth infections and a sore mouth.
note: Search summary of NHS beclometasone pages: rinse mouth or brush teeth after using a steroid inhaler to prevent infections and a sore mouth.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK gives similar advice, saying to rinse the mouth with water and spit it out if the inhaler contains steroid.
note: Spacer video summary: if the inhaler contains steroid, rinse the mouth with water and spit it out.

sentence: The NHS adds that using a spacer with a beclometasone inhaler can also help prevent side effects in the mouth.
note: Search summary: using a spacer with beclometasone inhaler can help prevent mouth side effects.

sentence: A reliever such as salbutamol is not a steroid, and the rinsing advice in these sources is for steroid inhalers.
note: Rinsing advice appears under steroid inhalers; author's inference stated cautiously.

sentence: The NHS says salbutamol has few side effects when used properly, and the common ones are shakiness, a faster heartbeat and headaches.
note: Search summary of NHS salbutamol side effects: few side effects when used properly; common ones shakiness, faster heartbeat, headaches.

sentence: It adds that these often ease or go away after the medicine has been used for a few days or weeks.
note: Search summary: side effects often improve and disappear after beta-2 agonists used for a few days or weeks.

sentence: Rarely, salbutamol can cause muscle pain, weakness or cramps, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be a sign of low potassium, and some people find the airways tighten after a dose.
note: Search summary: rare serious effects incl. muscle pain/weakness/cramps or irregular heartbeat linked with low potassium; paradoxical bronchospasm can occur.

sentence: For beclometasone, the NHS lists oral thrush, a sore or dry throat and a hoarse voice as the most frequent effects.
note: Search summary: oral thrush and dry/sore throat or hoarse voice are the most frequent.

sentence: If thrush develops, the NHS says a pharmacist can suggest an antifungal mouth gel, and the inhaler is still used while the gel is used.
note: Search summary: pharmacist can suggest an antifungal mouth gel; keep using the inhaler while using the antifungal.

sentence: A pharmacist or GP can advise on non-urgent side effects.
note: Route to advice is the site's signposting rule; pharmacist suggestion on thrush from NHS beclometasone page.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or for new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain after salbutamol.
note: Search summaries: call 999 for new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain, or signs of serious allergic reaction such as swelling of lips, mouth, throat or tongue.

sentence: If too much salbutamol has been used and the heartbeat is fast or noticeable, the NHS says to contact NHS 111.
note: Search summary: if you take too much and have a fast or noticeable heartbeat, contact 111.

sentence: The NHS says needing salbutamol more often than usual may mean the condition is getting worse and that different treatment is needed.
note: Search summary: needing it more than usual (the page gave a count which is left out here) may mean the condition is worsening and different treatment needed.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says that regularly needing a reliever inhaler is a sign that asthma is not well controlled, and it advises seeing the GP or asthma nurse.
note: Search summary of Asthma + Lung UK action plan guidance: needing reliever regularly is a sign asthma is not well controlled; see GP or asthma nurse. The page gave a weekly count, which is left out. Page is for healthcare professionals; reliever page also says frequent need signals a problem.

sentence: The NHS likewise advises speaking to a GP or asthma nurse if symptoms continue while using a preventer.
note: Search summary: speak to a GP or asthma nurse if you continue to have symptoms while using a preventer.

sentence: This is usually a reason for a routine asthma review rather than an emergency, although a sudden worsening is different, as the next section sets out.
note: Author's linking sentence: review routes from sources above; emergencies in the next section.

sentence: The NHS and Asthma + Lung UK say that during an asthma attack a person uses their reliever inhaler as set out in their plan and calls 999 for an ambulance if the reliever is not helping.
note: Search summary of NHS-style asthma attack pages (nhsinform, Asthma + Lung UK asthma-attacks page): if reliever not helping, call 999 and say it is an asthma attack. Puff counts in the source are left out.

sentence: They say to call 999 as well if symptoms get worse at any point, or if there is worry at any time, or if there is no reliever inhaler and breathing is a struggle.
note: Search summary: call 999 if feel worse at any point, do not feel better, are worried, or have no reliever inhaler and struggling to breathe.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says a person who feels able to get to hospital should still call 999, so treatment can begin on the way.
note: Search summary: even if able to get to A&E yourself, call 999 for an ambulance so you can be treated on the way.

sentence: After an attack, it says to ask for an urgent same-day appointment with the GP or nurse if the person managed it alone.
note: Search summary: if managed the attack yourself with reliever, ask for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment.

sentence: For urgent advice that is not an emergency, NHS 111 is the route, and a GP appointment suits routine questions and the yearly asthma review.
note: NHS 111 for urgent advice from the salbutamol page (too much used); annual asthma review from the Asthma + Lung UK spacers page; remainder is the site's signposting rule.
